title: Mother braces for inquest; Son died after pepper-spraying by Toronto police Family denied legal aid to have lawyer present: [ONT Edition]
article: For Maria Blentzas, the death of her son Nicholas means a life sentence of sadness.

"Everybody did wrong against Nick," Blentzas told the Toronto Star as she choked back tears and wiped the smudged mascara under her eyes with a tissue. "Everyone involved did wrong. He got the conviction of death and they gave us the conviction to be sad the rest of our lives."

An inquest into the death of 24-year-old Nicholas Blentzas, who had a history of mental illness and died after being handcuffed and pepper-sprayed by Toronto police on June 23, 2002, is scheduled to begin today.
The province's Special Investigations Unit cleared the police of any wrongdoing, but an inquest has been called, as is the case with most deaths that occur in police custody.

When the coroner's court opens its doors this morning, the family's interests won't be officially represented because their request for legal aid has been denied. And Maria Blentzas, fearful of attending without a lawyer, won't be there. Highly emotional, she is worried that she might collapse listening to the evidence. Instead, two of her children will be there, listening and taking notes.

Lawyer Suzan Fraser, who had hoped to represent the family, was shocked by the decision not to grant legal aid, but said whether someone has legal counsel at an inquest is discretionary. She plans to appeal the decision, fearful that the concerns of the Blentzas family won't be heard.

"It's an intimidating forum for anyone, let alone an unsophisticated family who was hoping to have counsel," said Fraser, who had wanted to raise several issues about the way police handle such cases, including crisis intervention versus police intervention, and the use of pepper spray on the mentally ill.

There have been a number of deaths involving the use of pepper spray by Toronto police in the past few years, including the case of Robert Walker, who was pepper-sprayed after he ran naked into the middle of an east-end street last year.
"There is some evidence that suggests people with mental illness are less likely to respond to pepper spray and are more susceptible to death," Fraser said.

The coroner's counsel, who can ask questions on behalf of the family, was not available to comment on the case. According to a source in the coroner's office, the inquest will focus on when people die in a state of excited delirium, which often occurs when the mentally ill go off their medication or when drug addicts or alcoholics suddenly stop using drugs or alcohol.

Things started to go awry for Nicholas at the end of high school, his mother said. He had planned to go to George Brown College to study electrical engineering, but after his sister plummeted to her death from a fifth-floor window, Nicholas began exhibiting symptoms of mental illness, Blentzas said.

"He was a nice, smart, good gentleman," she said yesterday in the living room of her Thorncliffe Park Dr. apartment. "He loved music. He was gifted in school; he was in the gifted program. He was very intelligent. He wasn't sick, to me, he was just depressed. After his sister's death, he went into a deep depression."

One night, Blentzas said, he told her he was going to jump off a bridge, and she took him to the hospital. Doctors suggested he might suffer from bipolar disorder or even schizophrenia, and the young man began taking medication.

Now, as Blentzas sits in her apartment more than 21/2 years after his death, she still can't believe her son is gone. "There was no reason for Nicholas to be dead right now, no reason at all," she sobbed, her voice slightly cracking. "What happened shouldn't have happened."

According to his mother, the week leading up to Nicholas's death had been troublesome. Earlier that week, police had been called to the apartment because Blentzas and Jim, Nicholas's brother, were concerned about him. He was acting oddly, and family members feared he was not taking his medication.
When police arrived, the family asked officers to take Nicholas to the hospital, but the police refused, Blentzas said.

A few days later, Nicholas locked himself out of the apartment, near Don Mills Rd. and Eglinton Ave. E., and was trying to break in with a fire extinguisher, his mother recounted. Neighbours in the building called police.

Officers peacefully escorted Nicholas downstairs, Blentzas said, but he ran away. Police chased Nicholas, who was caught, handcuffed and pepper-sprayed, she said. By the time the ambulance arrived, he was dead. The cause of death was cardiac arrest.
But to Blentzas, none of it makes any sense. And she wants the inquest to ensure that what happened to her family won't happen to someone else.
"I have five grandchildren and they'll have children. I don't want that to happen again - not to anybody, not just my family."
